entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Very good, detailed knowledge of how something works or why it happens, beyond the basic facts.
entries.usage: Common in education, job ads, interviews and academic writing. Patterns are *have / gain / develop a deep understanding of* + noun, and the comparative *a deeper understanding of* is very common after *gain* or *give*. The preposition is *of*; *a good understanding* is more modest.
entries.pattern: have / gain / develop a deep understanding of + noun
examples: After twenty years as a mechanic, he has **a deep understanding of** how engines work.
Living abroad for a year gave her **a deeper understanding of** her own culture.
The job requires **a deep understanding of** statistics and some experience with Python.

drill.sentence: Growing up on a farm gave my mother {{a deep understanding of}} animals and the weather.
drill.hint: very detailed knowledge of (the adjective is not *good*, *real* or *thorough*)

mistake.wrong: He has a deep understanding for physics.
mistake.right: He has a deep understanding of physics.
mistake.why: German *Verständnis für* tempts learners to use *for*; for knowledge, English says *understanding of*.

entries.related: *a good grasp of* — solid understanding, less deep; *an in-depth knowledge of* — detailed knowledge; *a superficial understanding* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To study a subject through a series of lessons or classes, for example at a college, a community center or online.
entries.usage: Very common in American English: *I'm taking a course in Spanish.* Patterns are *take a course in / on* + subject and *take a class*, which Americans often use for a single course. The verb is *take*; British speakers also say *do a course*.
entries.pattern: take a course in / on + subject
examples: I'm **taking a course** in photography at the community college on Tuesday nights.
Before we adopted the puppy, we **took a short course** on dog training.
Many nurses **take a course** in sign language so they can communicate with deaf patients.

drill.sentence: Before our trip to Mexico, my wife and I {{took a course}} in conversational Spanish.
drill.hint: studied in a series of lessons (the verb is not *did*; the noun is not *class*)

mistake.wrong: Last year I visited a course in Spanish.
mistake.right: Last year I took a course in Spanish.
mistake.why: German *einen Kurs besuchen* is *take a course* in English; *visit* means going somewhere for a short time.

entries.related: *take a class* — very common in American English; *sign up for* / *enroll in* — register for a course; *drop a course* — stop taking it.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Being officially examined, for example by the police, a government agency or an employer, in order to find out the facts.
entries.usage: Common in news, legal and official language. Patterns are *be under investigation (for* + offense*)*, *remain under investigation* and *The cause is under investigation*. There is usually no article before *investigation*.
entries.pattern: be / remain under investigation (by + agency / for + offense)
examples: The cause of the fire is still **under investigation**, but police don't suspect arson.
Two employees are **under investigation** for stealing from the company.
The restaurant was **under investigation** after dozens of customers got food poisoning.

drill.sentence: The coach has been suspended while the team's finances are {{under investigation}}.
drill.hint: being officially looked into (the noun is not *review* or *audit*)

entries.related: *under review* — being checked, often a decision or policy; *look into* — informal, investigate; *be cleared* — the opposite, found not guilty after an investigation.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have a period away from work or school, often traveling somewhere to rest or have fun.
entries.usage: Very common in American English; British speakers say *go on holiday*. Patterns are *take a vacation*, *take a week of vacation* and *go on vacation*. Americans use *holiday* mostly for public holidays like Thanksgiving, and *the holidays* for the season around Christmas.
entries.pattern: take a vacation; take (two weeks of) vacation; go on vacation
examples: We haven't **taken a vacation** in three years, so we're finally going to Hawaii in March.
My boss never **takes a vacation**, and she seems to expect the rest of us to do the same.
If you're feeling burned out, maybe it's time to **take a vacation**.

drill.sentence: I'm exhausted; once this busy season ends, I'm going to {{take a vacation}} somewhere with no Wi-Fi.
drill.hint: have some time off, probably traveling (the noun is not *break* or *trip*; the verb is not *go on*)

mistake.wrong: We're making vacation in Spain this summer.
mistake.right: We're taking a vacation in Spain this summer.
mistake.why: German *Urlaub machen* is *take a vacation* or *go on vacation* in English; *make* is wrong here.

entries.related: *go on vacation* — same meaning, focuses on leaving; *take time off* — be away from work, not necessarily traveling; *staycation* — a vacation spent at home.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A high level of knowledge and skill in a language or a subject, so that you can use it easily and correctly.
entries.usage: Typical of résumés, job ads and formal evaluations, and used mainly about languages: *a good command of English*. Patterns are *have a good / excellent / strong command of* + noun. It sounds formal, so in conversation people say *speak Spanish well* or *be fluent in Spanish*.
entries.pattern: have a good / excellent command of + language / subject
examples: Applicants must have **a good command of** both English and French.
After a year in Madrid, she had **a surprisingly good command of** Spanish.
The young lawyer showed **a good command of** the facts during the trial.

drill.sentence: My neighbor moved here from Poland at forty, but he already has {{a good command of}} English and reads the local paper every morning.
drill.hint: he can use the language well (the plainest adjective, not *great* or *excellent*; the noun is not *grasp* or *knowledge*)

mistake.wrong: I have good knowledges in English.
mistake.right: I have a good command of English.
mistake.why: *Knowledge* is uncountable; for languages, English says *a good command of* or *a good knowledge of*.

entries.related: *fluent in* — able to speak a language easily; *a working knowledge of* — enough to use it in practice; *a good grasp of* — good understanding, often of a subject.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To talk honestly about something, without hiding facts or feelings, often a subject people usually avoid.
entries.usage: Common in interviews, journalism and conversation about health, money, family or personal problems. Patterns are *speak openly about* + noun or *-ing* and *speak openly with* someone; *talk openly* is equally common and a little more casual. It often suggests courage, because the topic is private or sensitive.
entries.pattern: speak / talk openly about + noun / -ing
examples: The actor has started to **speak openly about** his struggle with depression.
In our family, we never **spoke openly about** money, so I didn't know how to budget.
It's important that kids feel they can **speak openly** with their parents about bullying.

drill.sentence: After her diagnosis, my aunt decided to {{speak openly about}} her illness with the whole family instead of keeping it a secret.
drill.hint: share the facts without hiding anything (the verb is not *talk*; the adverb is not *frankly* or *honestly*)

entries.related: *be open about* — not hide something; *speak frankly* — say exactly what you think, even if it is unwelcome; *keep something quiet* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To do things that could have bad results, usually because you hope for a good result.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, business, sports and advice. Patterns are *take risks (with* + noun*)*, *take a risk* for one decision and *take the risk of* + *-ing*. *Take chances* is a common informal alternative, and *risk-taking* is the noun.
entries.pattern: take risks (with + noun); take a risk; take the risk of + -ing
examples: My grandmother **took a huge risk** when she moved to New York with fifty dollars in her pocket.
Don't **take risks** with your health; see a doctor if the pain comes back.
Young drivers tend to **take more risks** on the road than older ones.

drill.sentence: My sister loves to {{take risks}}: she's tried skydiving, bungee jumping and cliff diving.
drill.hint: do things that could go badly (the noun is not *chances*)

entries.related: *take chances* — informal, similar; *a calculated risk* — a risk you take after careful thought; *play it safe* — the opposite, avoid risks.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Someone who learns new skills or information quickly.
entries.usage: Common in job interviews, résumés, sports and conversation about children. It is a compliment, and people often say it about themselves in interviews: *I'm a fast learner.* *A quick learner* means the same; *a slow learner* is the opposite and can sound unkind.
entries.pattern: be a fast / quick learner
examples: Our new hire had never used the software before, but she's **a fast learner**.
My grandson is **a fast learner**; he figured out the TV remote before he could talk.
In job interviews, I always say I'm **a fast learner**, which is true but probably what everyone says.

drill.sentence: Grandpa got his first smartphone in May and turned out to be {{a fast learner}}: by June, he was sending us videos every day.
drill.hint: someone who picks things up quickly (the adjective is not *quick*; not *a quick study*)

entries.related: *a quick learner* — same; *a quick study* — same meaning, mainly American; *pick things up* — informal, learn easily.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Being examined in order to decide whether to approve, change or continue something.
entries.usage: Common at work, in government and in official notices, often about policies, applications, budgets and contracts: *Your application is under review.* Patterns are *be / remain under review* and *come under review*. Unlike *under investigation*, it suggests checking or reconsidering, not a suspected crime.
entries.pattern: be / remain under review
examples: Your application is currently **under review**, and we'll contact you within two weeks.
The school's cell phone policy is **under review** after complaints from parents.
The referee's call is **under review**, so the crowd is waiting to see if the goal counts.

drill.sentence: The city's plan to close two libraries is still {{under review}}, so nothing has been decided yet.
drill.hint: being examined before a decision (the noun is not *consideration* or *discussion*)

entries.related: *under consideration* — being thought about; *up for review* — due to be reviewed soon; *finalized* — the opposite, already decided.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start an official process in court against a person or organization, for example by suing them.
entries.usage: Formal; typical of news, letters from lawyers, contracts and official warnings: *We will take legal action if …* Patterns are *take legal action against* someone and *threaten (to take) legal action*. In conversation, Americans more often say *sue* someone.
entries.pattern: take legal action against + someone
examples: If the landlord doesn't return your deposit, you can **take legal action** against him.
The singer is **taking legal action** against a company that used her song without permission.
Several families **took legal action** against the chemical plant after their wells were polluted.

drill.sentence: The photographer threatened to {{take legal action}} if the magazine kept using her pictures without paying.
drill.hint: start a court case (not *sue* or *go to court*)

entries.related: *sue* — the plain verb, more common in speech; *take someone to court* — similar, less formal; *settle out of court* — agree before a trial.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A subject that many people are discussing or arguing about at the moment.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, conversation and business. Patterns are *a hot topic (of conversation / debate)* and *a hot topic among* + group. It suggests the subject is current and often a little controversial; *a hot-button issue* is stronger and makes people angry.
entries.pattern: a hot topic (of conversation) among + group
examples: Working from home is still **a hot topic** in many offices.
The new parking rules were **a hot topic** at the neighborhood meeting last night.
The finale of the show became **a hot topic** of conversation online.

drill.sentence: Rising rent is {{a hot topic}} among young people in the city right now.
drill.hint: something everyone is talking about (the adjective is not *big*; not *a talking point*)

entries.related: *a hot-button issue* — a topic that makes people angry; *the talk of the town* — something everyone in a place is discussing; *old news* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start to work, or to start to apply officially; used for laws, rules, price changes and medicines.
entries.usage: Common in news, official notices and medicine. Patterns are *take effect on* + date (Americans often drop *on*: *take effect January 1*) and *take effect immediately*; for medicine, informal *kick in* is also common. Don't confuse it with *have an effect on*, which means to influence something.
entries.pattern: take effect (on + date / immediately)
examples: The new speed limit **takes effect** on Monday, so watch for the signs.
The painkillers took about twenty minutes to **take effect**.
The price increase **takes effect** January first, so stock up on coffee now.

drill.sentence: I took the allergy pill an hour ago, but it still hasn't {{taken effect}}.
drill.hint: begun to produce its result (not *kicked in* or *worked*)

mistake.wrong: The new rules take affect on Monday.
mistake.right: The new rules take effect on Monday.
mistake.why: *Effect* is the noun here; *affect* is normally a verb.

entries.related: *go into effect* — same, common in American news; *come into force* — formal, mostly for laws; *kick in* — informal, start working, often of medicine.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To enjoy something very much, from start to finish.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews, thank-you notes and emails; it sounds warm and a little more educated than *really enjoy*. It takes a noun or an *-ing* form: *I thoroughly enjoyed meeting you.* Like *enjoy* itself, it always needs an object.
entries.pattern: thoroughly enjoy + noun / -ing
examples: We **thoroughly enjoyed** our stay; the staff couldn't have been friendlier.
The kids **thoroughly enjoyed** splashing in every puddle on the way home.
I **thoroughly enjoyed** your talk last night, especially the part about sleep.

drill.sentence: Thank you for dinner last night; we {{thoroughly enjoyed}} the food and the company.
drill.hint: liked very much, from start to finish (the adverb is not *really* or *truly*)

mistake.wrong: We thoroughly enjoyed at the party.
mistake.why: *Enjoy* needs an object: *enjoy the party* or *enjoy ourselves*.

entries.related: *really enjoy* — plainer, more casual; *have a great time* — enjoy an event; *can't stand* — the opposite, strongly dislike.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A subject that may upset, embarrass or offend people, so it must be discussed carefully.
entries.usage: Common at work, in journalism, medicine and family life. Patterns are *a sensitive issue for* someone and *handle / approach a sensitive issue (carefully)*; *a delicate matter* is similar but more formal. *Sensitive* here describes the topic, not a person who is easily hurt.
entries.pattern: a sensitive issue (for + someone); handle a sensitive issue
examples: Money is **a sensitive issue** in my family, so we never talk about salaries.
The doctor handled the **sensitive issue** of my father's memory loss with real kindness.
Layoffs are always **a sensitive issue**, so the manager spoke to each employee in private.

drill.sentence: Weight can be {{a sensitive issue}} for teenagers, so think carefully before you comment on it.
drill.hint: a subject that can easily hurt feelings (the adjective is not *delicate* or *touchy*; the noun is not *topic* or *subject*)

entries.related: *a touchy subject* — informal, same; *a sore point* — something that still makes someone upset; *a delicate matter* — formal, needs tact.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start an official job, especially an elected position such as mayor, governor or sheriff.
entries.usage: Typical of news and formal writing. There is no article: *take office*, *since taking office*, *before she took office*. *In office* means currently holding the job, and *leave office* is the opposite.
entries.pattern: take office (in + month / on + date)
examples: The new mayor will **take office** in January.
Since **taking office**, the school board president has visited every school in the district.
Many leaders find the job much harder than they expected once they **take office**.

drill.sentence: The new sheriff will officially {{take office}} on Monday, after a short ceremony at the courthouse.
drill.hint: begin the official job (not *be sworn in*)

mistake.wrong: The new mayor took the office in May.
mistake.right: The new mayor took office in May.
mistake.why: In this phrase, *office* means an official position and takes no article.

entries.related: *be sworn in* — formally promise to do the job at a ceremony; *in office* — currently holding the job; *leave office* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An inability to concentrate on one thing for long before getting bored or distracted.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, parenting, teaching and talk about phones and media. Patterns are *have a short attention span* and *shorter attention spans*; people often say it humorously about themselves. *Span* here means a length of time.
entries.pattern: have a short attention span
examples: Toddlers have **a short attention span**, so story time lasts ten minutes at most.
I have **a short attention span** for podcasts; after five minutes I start cleaning the kitchen.
Many teachers worry that phones are giving students **shorter attention spans**.

drill.sentence: My puppy has {{a short attention span}}, so we keep his training sessions really brief.
drill.hint: can't focus for long (the noun is not *fuse*, which is about anger)

entries.related: *easily distracted* — similar adjective phrase; *a short fuse* — a quick temper, not about focus; *laser focus* — informal, the opposite.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Not available in large enough amounts to meet the need.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and conversation about goods, workers, money or time. It usually follows *be*: *Nurses are in short supply.* With abstract nouns it often sounds humorous: *Patience was in short supply.*
entries.pattern: be in short supply
examples: Fresh vegetables are **in short supply** on the island during the winter.
Qualified nurses are **in short supply** in many rural hospitals.
By the end of the eight-hour drive, patience was **in short supply** in the back seat.

drill.sentence: After the storm, bottled water and batteries were {{in short supply}} at every store in town.
drill.hint: not available in large enough amounts (not *scarce*, *running low* or *hard to find*)

entries.related: *scarce* — the one-word equivalent, a bit more formal; *run low (on)* — have only a little left; *plentiful* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To accept a lower salary or wage for doing your job.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, business news and sports. Patterns are *take a pay cut* and *take a twenty percent pay cut*; it often suggests a sacrifice, for example to keep a job or to do work you love. A company *cuts* someone's pay; the employee *takes* the cut.
entries.pattern: take a (20 percent) pay cut
examples: She **took a pay cut** to work for a nonprofit, but she says she's much happier now.
During the slow season, everyone at the restaurant **took a pay cut** so nobody had to be laid off.
The star quarterback **took a pay cut** so the team could afford to keep its best receivers.

drill.sentence: I'd rather {{take a pay cut}} than spend two more years working for that terrible boss.
drill.hint: agree to earn less money (verb + noun; the verb is not *accept*)

entries.related: *get a raise* — the opposite, earn more (British *a pay rise*); *take a hit* — informal, suffer a loss; *be laid off* — lose your job because there isn't enough work.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Facts or physical proof that clearly show that something is true, not just opinions or suspicions.
entries.usage: Common in law, journalism, science and everyday arguments. Typical frames are *There's no hard evidence (that / of …)* and *need / find hard evidence*; it is very often negative. *Evidence* is uncountable, so it takes no *an* and has no plural.
entries.pattern: (no) hard evidence of + noun / that + clause
examples: Police suspect him, but they don't have any **hard evidence** yet.
There's no **hard evidence** that drinking eight glasses of water a day is necessary.
I'm sure my roommate is eating my cereal; I just need some **hard evidence** before I say anything.

drill.sentence: Lots of people believe full moons make kids act wild, but there's no {{hard evidence}} for it.
drill.hint: facts that really prove it (the adjective is not *solid*, *concrete* or *scientific*)

mistake.why: *Evidence* is uncountable, so it has no plural; for several items, say *pieces of evidence*.

entries.related: *proof* — evidence that shows something is definitely true; *circumstantial evidence* — evidence that suggests but doesn't prove; *hearsay* — things heard from others, not proof.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To put a lot of money, time or effort into something, hoping for a good result later.
entries.usage: Common in business news, finance, sports and talk about personal decisions. The pattern is *invest heavily in* + noun or *-ing*; *heavily* can also come before the verb (*heavily invest in*), but after the verb is more common. *Be heavily invested in* often describes emotional effort: *She was heavily invested in the relationship.*
entries.pattern: invest heavily in + noun / -ing
examples: The city has **invested heavily in** bike lanes and public transit over the past ten years.
Our parents **invested heavily in** our education, so we never took expensive vacations.
The club **invested heavily in** young players, and it's finally paying off.

drill.sentence: Grandpa {{invested heavily in}} one company's stock and lost most of his savings when it collapsed.
drill.hint: spent a big part of his savings on (the verb is not *bet*; the adverb is not *a lot*)

entries.related: *pour money into* — informal, invest a lot, sometimes wastefully; *bet heavily on* — risk a lot on one outcome; *cut back on* — the opposite, reduce spending on.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To create enough space for something or someone, usually by moving or removing other things.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday conversation about homes, cars, schedules and lives. The pattern is *make room for* + noun or someone; *room* here is uncountable and means space, so there is no article. It is also used for time and life: *make room in your schedule for* something.
entries.pattern: make room for + noun / someone
examples: We moved the couch against the wall to **make room for** the Christmas tree.
Can you scoot over and **make room for** Grandma on the bench?
The old factory was torn down to **make room for** new apartments.

drill.sentence: I'm getting rid of half my clothes to {{make room for}} the baby's things in the closet.
drill.hint: leave enough area free for (the noun after the verb is not *space*)

mistake.wrong: Can you make place for me on the couch?
mistake.right: Can you make room for me on the couch?
mistake.why: German *Platz machen* is *make room* in English; *place* means a location, not free space.

entries.related: *make space for* — very similar; *clear out* — remove things to free up space; *take up room* — the opposite, fill space.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that happens because of one specific cause, with no other step or cause in between.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports, academic writing and serious conversation. Patterns are *be a direct result of* + noun and *as a direct result of* + noun at the start of a sentence. *Direct* stresses that the link is clear and immediate; with *indirect*, the link is weaker.
entries.pattern: (as) a direct result of + noun / -ing
examples: The flooding was **a direct result of** heavy rain and blocked drains.
**As a direct result of** the factory closing, half the shops on Main Street went out of business.
Her promotion was **a direct result of** the way she handled last year's crisis.

drill.sentence: My back pain is {{a direct result of}} sitting at a bad desk ten hours a day.
drill.hint: the immediate outcome of (not *due to* or *caused by*; the noun is not *consequence*)

mistake.wrong: The delay was a direct result from the strike.
mistake.right: The delay was a direct result of the strike.
mistake.why: The noun *result* takes *of*; *from* goes with the verb: *result from*.

entries.related: *a consequence of* — similar, often negative; *a by-product of* — an extra, unplanned result; *a coincidence* — the opposite, no causal link.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To help to achieve, produce or improve something together with other people; it can also mean to give money.
entries.usage: Common at work, in science, community life and fundraising. Patterns are *make a (big / major / valuable) contribution to* + noun and *make a contribution of* + amount; *contribute to* is the shorter verb form. In speeches and thank-you notes, *valuable* and *significant* are typical adjectives.
entries.pattern: make a (valuable / major) contribution to + noun
examples: Every volunteer **made a contribution to** the new playground, even if it was just painting a fence.
Her research **made a major contribution to** our understanding of sleep.
If you'd like to **make a contribution to** the teachers' holiday gift, please send it in by Friday.

drill.sentence: Everyone on our street {{made a contribution to}} the fund for the family who lost their home in the fire.
drill.hint: helped with money for (verb + noun; the noun is not *donation*; not *contributed to*)

entries.related: *contribute to* — the one-verb version; *play a part in* — help, often less formally; *chip in* — informal, give a little money or help.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Responsible for a mistake, an accident or a problem.
entries.usage: Common in insurance, law, news and arguments about who caused something: *Which driver was at fault?* It follows *be* or a noun (*the driver at fault*), with no article. It is a little more formal than *It's his fault*, and *to blame* is very close.
entries.pattern: be at fault (for + noun / -ing)
examples: The insurance company decided the other driver was **at fault**, so they paid for our repairs.
When a marriage ends, it's rarely just one person who's **at fault**.
If the app crashes because of a bug, the developers are **at fault**, not the users.

drill.sentence: After the collision on the ice, both hockey players insisted the other one was {{at fault}}.
drill.hint: the one who caused the problem (not *to blame* or *responsible*)

entries.related: *to blame* — very similar; *in the wrong* — having behaved badly or unfairly; *blameless* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An effect that continues for a long time after the event or person that caused it.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, journalism, education and tributes. The pattern is *have / leave a lasting impact on* + someone or something, with *on* as the preposition. *A lasting impression* is different: it is about what people remember.
entries.pattern: have / leave a lasting impact on + someone / something
examples: My high school chemistry teacher had **a lasting impact on** how I think about the world.
The hurricane left **a lasting impact on** the town; some families never moved back.
Stress in early childhood can have **a lasting impact** on adult health.

drill.sentence: Living in Japan for a year as a teenager had {{a lasting impact}} on my brother's career choices.
drill.hint: an effect that stayed with him for years (the adjective is not *long-term* or *profound*; the noun is not *effect*)

entries.related: *a lasting impression* — a memory that stays; *a long-term effect* — plainer; *a fleeting effect* — the opposite, short-lived.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To promise firmly to do something or to support someone, often over a long time.
entries.usage: Common in relationships, at work, in sports and in public promises. Patterns are *make a commitment to* + noun, *-ing* or verb, and *make a long-term / serious commitment*. In relationships, *commitment* often means marriage or a serious partnership, so *afraid of commitment* is a common phrase.
entries.pattern: make a (long-term) commitment (to + noun / -ing / verb)
examples: Getting a dog means **making a commitment** for the next fifteen years.
He's thirty-five and still afraid to **make a commitment** to anyone.
The company **made a commitment** to cut its plastic waste in half by 2030.

drill.sentence: Before you join the choir, remember that you're {{making a commitment}} to every Thursday rehearsal for a year.
drill.hint: promising to be there regularly (verb + noun; not *signing up*)

entries.related: *commit to* — the verb form; *make a promise* — plainer, often for one action; *back out (of)* — the opposite, break an agreement.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To urge someone firmly to do something, making clear that you think it is important.
entries.usage: Common in emails, official notices, teaching and advice: *We strongly encourage all guests to book early.* The pattern is *strongly encourage someone to* + verb, or *strongly encourage* + *-ing*; the passive *be strongly encouraged to* is typical of notices. It is polite but firm, softer than *require*.
entries.pattern: strongly encourage someone to + verb; be strongly encouraged to + verb
examples: We **strongly encourage** all parents to attend the meeting about the new school schedule.
My doctor **strongly encouraged** me to cut back on coffee.
Hikers are **strongly encouraged** to carry extra water in the summer months.

drill.sentence: The hotel {{strongly encourages}} guests to make a dinner reservation early, because the restaurant fills up fast.
drill.hint: pushes, in a polite but firm way (the verb is not *recommends*, *advises* or *urges*)

entries.related: *strongly recommend* — similar, more about advice; *urge* — stronger, sometimes emotional; *discourage* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A worry that more and more people share, or that becomes more serious over time.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and formal speech about health, safety, money and the environment. Patterns are *a growing concern for* + group, *growing concern about / over* + noun and *There is growing concern that …*, the last two without *a*. It sounds measured and neutral.
entries.pattern: a growing concern (for + group); growing concern about + noun / that …
examples: Loneliness among older people is **a growing concern** for doctors.
There's **growing concern** that the old dam won't survive another major flood.
Residents have expressed **growing concern** about speeding cars near the elementary school.

drill.sentence: Ticks that carry Lyme disease are {{a growing concern}} as winters get warmer in the Northeast.
drill.hint: a worry that is getting bigger (the adjective is not *rising* or *increasing*; the noun is not *problem*)

entries.related: *mounting concern* — similar, more formal; *a cause for concern* — a reason to worry; *a non-issue* — the opposite, nothing to worry about.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To say that something is true, often without giving proof.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, law, science, advertising and arguments. Patterns are *make the claim that …* and *make claims about* + noun; adjectives like *bold*, *false* and *wild* are typical. A different sense is asking an insurance company for money, which Americans usually call *filing a claim*.
entries.pattern: make a (bold / false) claim (that … / about + noun)
examples: The ad **makes the claim** that this cream removes wrinkles in a week, which I seriously doubt.
My nephew **made the bold claim** that he could eat twenty hot dogs in ten minutes.
Scientists shouldn't **make claims** they can't support with data.

drill.sentence: Before you {{make a claim}} like that in public, be sure you can prove it.
drill.hint: state that something is true (the noun is not *statement* or *accusation*)

entries.related: *allege* — formal, claim wrongdoing without proof; *assert* — state firmly; *back up a claim* — support it with evidence.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be responsible for something bad that has happened.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and discussion of problems. Patterns are *be to blame for* + noun and *Who's to blame?*; *partly* or *largely* often goes before *to blame*. The active form *to blame* is normal even though the meaning is passive; *to be blamed* is possible but less common.
entries.pattern: be (partly / largely) to blame for + noun; who's to blame?
examples: A broken signal was **to blame for** this morning's subway delays.
Don't look at me; I'm not **to blame for** the mess in the kitchen.
Doctors say poor sleep is **partly to blame for** the rise in teenage anxiety.

drill.sentence: The coach said the referees were {{to blame for}} the loss, but everyone knew his team had played badly.
drill.hint: the cause of the problem (not *responsible for* or *at fault*)

entries.related: *at fault* — responsible for a mistake, common in insurance; *take the blame* — accept responsibility, fairly or not; *blameless* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To plan and prepare the details of something, such as a trip, an event or care for someone.
entries.usage: Common in emails, travel, work and family life. Patterns are *make arrangements for* + noun or someone *to* + verb, and *make arrangements with* someone; the noun is usually plural. *Travel, funeral* and *childcare arrangements* are typical combinations.
entries.pattern: make arrangements for + noun / with + someone
examples: We've **made arrangements** for my sister to pick up the kids from school on Friday.
If you need a wheelchair at the airport, please **make arrangements** with the airline in advance.
After her father died, she flew home to **make the funeral arrangements**.

drill.sentence: Before we leave for two weeks, we need to {{make arrangements}} for someone to feed the cat.
drill.hint: work out the details (verb + noun; not *arrange*; the noun is not *plans*)

entries.related: *arrange* — the one-word verb; *make plans* — more general and casual; *make preparations* — get ready, often with practical work.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The usual, accepted way of doing something in a particular job, field or organization.
entries.usage: Common at work, in law, medicine and business, and often used to reassure someone: *Don't worry, it's standard practice.* Patterns are *It's standard practice (for* someone*) to* + verb and *standard practice in* + field, usually without an article. It sounds neutral and official.
entries.pattern: It's standard practice (for someone) to + verb
examples: It's **standard practice** for hospitals to check a patient's name and date of birth before every procedure.
The landlord asked for two months' rent up front, which he said was **standard practice**.
Checking references is **standard practice** when hiring, so don't be surprised if they call your old boss.

drill.sentence: In most American diners, it's {{standard practice}} to bring customers a glass of water as soon as they sit down.
drill.hint: the accepted way things are done (the adjective is not *common*, *normal* or *usual*; not *customary*)

entries.related: *common practice* — what many people do, less official; *the norm* — the usual situation; *best practices* — the methods known to work best.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To say no to an offer, an invitation or a request in a polite way.
entries.usage: Common in emails, etiquette advice and stories. *Decline* is more formal than *say no* or *turn down*, and it takes a noun (*decline the invitation*) or *to* + verb (*decline to answer*). In emails, people often write *I'm afraid I'll have to decline* to sound gracious.
entries.pattern: politely decline + offer / invitation; politely decline to + verb
examples: She offered me a second piece of cake, but I **politely declined**.
The actor **politely declined** to answer questions about his divorce.
I had to **politely decline** the job offer because the salary was too low.

drill.sentence: My neighbor invited me to his three-hour slideshow of vacation photos, but I {{politely declined}}.
drill.hint: said no, but nicely (adverb + verb; not *refused* or *turned it down*)

entries.related: *turn down* — less formal, say no to an offer; *refuse* — stronger, can sound rude; *gladly accept* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To complain, worry or get excited too much about something that is not important.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often in the negative: *Don't make a fuss.* Patterns are *make a (big) fuss about / over* + noun; *make a fuss over* someone (British *of*) means to give them a lot of attention, which can be positive. *Kick up a fuss* is a stronger, noisier version.
entries.pattern: make a (big) fuss about / over + noun
examples: It's just a small scratch on the car; there's no need to **make a fuss about** it.
My dad hates it when people **make a big fuss about** his birthday.
One customer **made a fuss** because his coffee wasn't hot enough, and the manager had to come out.

drill.sentence: The waiter brought me the wrong soup, but I didn't want to {{make a fuss}}, so I just ate it.
drill.hint: complain about something minor (the noun is not *scene* or *big deal*; the verb is not *kick up*)

entries.related: *make a scene* — behave loudly or emotionally in public; *kick up a fuss* — complain loudly; *take something in stride* — the opposite, stay calm about a problem.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The methods or ways of working that are known to give the best results in a field.
entries.usage: Common in business, health care, education and tech, and sometimes mocked as corporate jargon. Patterns are *follow best practices*, *best practices for* + noun or *-ing* and *share best practices*. In American English the plural is the usual form, though *It's best practice to* + verb is also used.
entries.pattern: follow / share best practices (for + noun / -ing)
examples: Our new manager wants every department to follow the same **best practices** for customer service.
After the outbreak, the hospital updated its **best practices** for preventing infections.
The bank's website has a list of **best practices** for keeping your passwords safe.

drill.sentence: The food safety class taught us {{best practices}} for handling raw chicken, such as using a separate cutting board.
drill.hint: proven methods that give the top results (not *guidelines* or *tips*)

entries.related: *standard practice* — the usual way, not necessarily the best; *guidelines* — official advice on what to do; *bad practice* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To give reasons, often weak or untrue ones, to avoid blame, responsibility or doing something.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, parenting, coaching and work, and usually critical: *Stop making excuses.* Patterns are *make excuses for* something or someone and *make an excuse to* + verb. The noun *excuse* ends in an /s/ sound, /ɪkˈskjus/, unlike the verb, /ɪkˈskjuz/.
entries.pattern: make excuses (for + noun / someone); make an excuse to + verb
examples: Stop **making excuses** and just tell me why you didn't call.
She keeps **making excuses for** her boyfriend, even though he's always late and never apologizes.
I **made an excuse** to leave the party early because I was exhausted.

drill.sentence: My brother always {{makes excuses}} when it's his turn to do the dishes: he's tired, he's busy, he's got a headache.
drill.hint: gives reasons to get out of it (the verb is not *finds* or *comes up with*)

entries.related: *come up with an excuse* — invent one; *a lame excuse* — informal, a weak excuse; *own up to* — the opposite, admit your fault.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person who is a friend of both you and another person.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and on social media, especially when explaining how people met: *We met through a mutual friend.* Patterns are *a mutual friend (of ours)*, *through a mutual friend* and *have mutual friends*. *Mutual* is the normal adjective here; *common friend* sounds non-native.
entries.pattern: a mutual friend (of ours); through a mutual friend
examples: Jake and I met through **a mutual friend** at a barbecue about ten years ago.
We have a lot of **mutual friends**, so it's awkward that we broke up.
I asked **a mutual friend** to find out whether she'd be open to meeting me for coffee.

drill.sentence: We didn't meet online; {{a mutual friend}} set us up on a blind date.
drill.hint: someone who knew both of us (the adjective is not *common* or *shared*)

mistake.wrong: We met through a common friend.
mistake.right: We met through a mutual friend.
mistake.why: German *ein gemeinsamer Freund* tempts learners to say *common friend*; natives say *mutual friend*.

entries.related: *a friend of a friend* — someone you know only through another person; *a shared interest* — something you both like; *a stranger* — the opposite.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Without a plan, pattern or reason, so that every person or thing has the same chance of being chosen.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, games, contests and news: *Winners will be chosen at random.* It usually follows the verb: *pick / choose / select* something *at random*. *Random* alone is an adjective (*a random number*), and in casual speech it can mean strange or unexpected: *That was so random.*
entries.pattern: pick / choose / select + something at random
examples: The teacher calls on students **at random**, so everyone has to pay attention.
I opened the cookbook **at random** and decided to make whatever was on that page.
Airport security picked my bag **at random** for an extra check.

drill.sentence: I didn't know any of the songs, so I picked one {{at random}} and hoped for the best.
drill.hint: without choosing on purpose (not *randomly*)

mistake.wrong: The winner was picked by random.
mistake.right: The winner was picked at random.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase is *at random*; *by* belongs to *by chance* and *by accident*.

entries.related: *randomly* — the adverb, same meaning; *by chance* — without planning, by luck; *on purpose* — the opposite, deliberately.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To say something formally and publicly, for example to the press, the police or a court.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and official situations. Patterns are *make a statement to* the police or the press and *make a public / formal statement*; organizations more often *issue* or *release a statement*. In another sense, *make a statement* can also mean to show your opinion or style without words: *Her red dress made a statement.*
entries.pattern: make a (public / formal) statement (to + the police / the press)
examples: After the accident, both drivers **made statements** to the police.
The hospital will **make a statement** about the patient's condition later this afternoon.
The victim's family **made a short statement** outside the courthouse, asking for privacy.

drill.sentence: The witness was asked to come to the station and {{make a statement}} about what she had seen.
drill.hint: formally describe it for the record (the verb is not *give*)

entries.related: *issue a statement* — official, usually written, from an organization; *give a statement* — similar, common with the police; *testify* — give evidence in court.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Received with real gratitude; a polite, formal way to thank someone or to ask for help.
entries.usage: Typical of emails, notices and formal requests: *Any help would be greatly appreciated.* It is passive, usually with *would be* in requests and *is / was / has been* in thanks. *Much appreciated* is a shorter, more casual version, common at the end of emails.
entries.pattern: (Any help) would be greatly appreciated; your support is greatly appreciated
examples: Any donations to the animal shelter would be **greatly appreciated**.
Your patience during the renovation has been **greatly appreciated**.
The extra help from parents during the school play was **greatly appreciated** by the teachers.

drill.sentence: If anyone has a spare winter coat for the coat drive, it would be {{greatly appreciated}}.
drill.hint: received with real thanks (the adverb is not *much* or *really*)

entries.related: *much appreciated* — shorter, more casual; *I'd be grateful if* — a polite request; *taken for granted* — the opposite, not valued.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To tell people officially or publicly about something, often something new or important.
entries.usage: Common at work, at school, at airports, in families and in the news. Patterns are *make an announcement about* + noun and *make an announcement that …*; *I have an announcement to make* often comes before big personal news, such as an engagement. Pilots and train staff *make announcements* over the speakers.
entries.pattern: make an announcement (about + noun / that …)
examples: At dinner, my sister stood up and said she had **an announcement to make**: she was pregnant.
The pilot **made an announcement** that we'd be landing twenty minutes late.
Every morning, the principal **makes announcements** over the loudspeaker before first period.

drill.sentence: Can I have everyone's attention? Before we cut the cake, the happy couple would like to {{make an announcement}}.
drill.hint: share some big news (verb + noun; the noun is not *toast* or *speech*)

entries.related: *announce* — the verb form; *make a statement* — more formal, often to the press; *keep something under wraps* — the opposite, keep it secret.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A small difference that is hard to notice or to explain.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, teaching, reviews and analysis. Patterns are *a subtle difference between A and B* and *There's a subtle difference*. *Slight* is only about size, while *subtle* suggests you need care or skill to notice the difference.
entries.pattern: a subtle difference between A and B
examples: There's **a subtle difference** between asking for feedback and asking for praise.
Only an expert could hear the **subtle differences** between the two violins.
My twin daughters look identical to strangers, but there are **subtle differences** in their smiles.

drill.sentence: Champagne and other sparkling wines taste the same to me, but my uncle insists there's {{a subtle difference}}.
drill.hint: a small distinction that's hard to notice (the adjective is not *slight* or *small*)

entries.related: *a fine line* — a very small difference between two things; *a slight difference* — small in size; *a world of difference* — the opposite, a huge difference.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make an important discovery, or suddenly make real progress, after a long period of effort.
entries.usage: Common in science, medicine and technology news, and also for police work, negotiations, therapy and personal goals. Patterns are *make a breakthrough in* + field or case and *make a major breakthrough*; *finally* often goes with it. *Have a breakthrough* is common for personal progress, and *achieve a breakthrough* is more formal.
entries.pattern: make a (major) breakthrough in + field / case
examples: Detectives finally **made a breakthrough** in the case when a neighbor's doorbell camera showed the car.
Scientists have **made a major breakthrough** in treating a rare childhood cancer.
Negotiators **made a breakthrough** late Sunday night, and the strike ended the next morning.

drill.sentence: My son struggled with reading for years, but this spring he {{made a breakthrough}} and now reads every night.
drill.hint: suddenly improved a lot (the verb is not *had*; not *turned a corner*)

entries.related: *turn a corner* — start to improve after a bad period; *make headway* — make progress; *hit a wall* — the opposite, get stuck.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Having a lot of training, experience and ability in a particular job or activity.
entries.usage: Common in job ads, economic news and descriptions of workers: *highly skilled workers / surgeons / welders*. Even before a noun it is usually written without a hyphen, because adverbs ending in *-ly* don't take one. The opposites are *unskilled* and *low-skilled*.
entries.pattern: a highly skilled + worker / surgeon; be highly skilled at + -ing
examples: The surgery was risky, but luckily she had a **highly skilled** surgeon.
My grandmother was **highly skilled** at sewing and made all of our Halloween costumes.
The factory struggles to find **highly skilled** welders, even though it pays well.

drill.sentence: Repairing antique clocks is slow, delicate work that only {{highly skilled}} craftsmen can do.
drill.hint: with a lot of training and talent (the adverb is not *very*; the participle is not *trained*)

entries.related: *highly trained* — stresses the training; *seasoned* — experienced; *unskilled* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Eating that includes the right amounts of different kinds of food, so the body gets all the nutrients it needs.
entries.usage: Common in health advice, school lessons, food packaging and conversation. Patterns are *eat / have / maintain a balanced diet* and *part of a balanced diet*, the second often in advertising. *Diet* here means what you normally eat, not a plan to lose weight.
entries.pattern: eat / maintain a balanced diet; part of a balanced diet
examples: Kids need **a balanced diet** with plenty of fruit, vegetables and protein to grow properly.
Doctors say most people who eat **a balanced diet** don't need extra vitamins.
The cereal box says it's "part of **a balanced diet**," but it's mostly sugar.

drill.sentence: Since he moved into his own apartment, my son has been living on pizza instead of eating {{a balanced diet}}.
drill.hint: the right mix of foods (the adjective is not *healthy* or *varied*)

entries.related: *a healthy diet* — similar, more general; *junk food* — unhealthy food; *go on a diet* — eat less to lose weight.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To become completely healthy again after an illness, an injury or an operation.
entries.usage: Common in news, medical updates and conversation: *Doctors expect him to make a full recovery.* The pattern is *make a full recovery (from* + illness or injury*)*; *recover fully* is the verb form. In get-well messages, people write *Wishing you a speedy recovery*.
entries.pattern: make a full recovery (from + illness / injury)
examples: The doctors say she'll **make a full recovery**, but she'll need a few weeks of rest.
After a bad fall from his bike, my uncle **made a full recovery** in just two months.
The team's star pitcher is expected to **make a full recovery** in time for the playoffs.

drill.sentence: The firefighter was badly burned, but after six months of treatment, he {{made a full recovery}}.
drill.hint: got completely healthy again (verb + adjective + noun; the adjective is not *complete*; not *recovered fully*)

entries.related: *recover fully* — the verb form; *bounce back* — informal, recover quickly; *on the mend* — informal, getting better.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: One after another, without a break.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, sports and news, after a number and a plural noun: *three days in a row*, *the fifth time in a row*. *Straight* is a casual alternative (*three nights straight*), and *consecutive* is more formal (*three consecutive days*). *In a row* can also be literal: things arranged in a line.
entries.pattern: number + plural noun + in a row; the third time in a row
examples: It's rained five days **in a row**, and the kids are going crazy inside.
Our team has lost four games **in a row**, so the coach might get fired.
This is the third time **in a row** you've forgotten to lock the front door.

drill.sentence: My neighbor's car alarm went off at three in the morning for the second night {{in a row}}.
drill.hint: one after another (not *straight* or *running*)

mistake.wrong: I worked three weekends after each other.
mistake.right: I worked three weekends in a row.
mistake.why: German *hintereinander* is *in a row* in English; *after each other* sounds unnatural here.

entries.related: *straight* — informal: *three nights straight*; *consecutive* — formal: *three consecutive wins*; *on and off* — the opposite, with breaks.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To improve or move toward a goal slowly but continuously, without big setbacks.
entries.usage: Common in school reports, medical updates, work updates and sports. Patterns are *make steady progress in / on / with* + noun and *make slow but steady progress*. *Progress* is uncountable, so it takes no *a* and has no plural.
entries.pattern: make (slow but) steady progress in / on / with + noun
examples: Since his stroke, my grandfather has **made steady progress** and can now walk with a cane.
Lucas has **made steady progress** in math this year, and his test scores show it.
Construction on the new subway line is **making steady progress**, despite the cold winter.

drill.sentence: I'm not fluent yet, but I've {{made steady progress}} with my Spanish by practicing a little every day.
drill.hint: improved slowly but constantly (the adjective is not *good* or *slow*)

mistake.wrong: She has made steady progresses this term.
mistake.right: She has made steady progress this term.
mistake.why: *Progress* is uncountable, so it has no plural.

entries.related: *make headway* — make progress, often against difficulty; *make strides* — make big progress; *stall* — the opposite, stop moving forward.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Extra costs that are not obvious at first and that you discover only later.
entries.usage: Common in consumer advice, business, travel and news, usually as a warning. Patterns are *the hidden costs of* + noun or *-ing*, *watch out for hidden costs* and *no hidden costs* in advertising. It can also mean costs that are not money, such as time or health.
entries.pattern: the hidden costs of + noun / -ing; no hidden costs
examples: The flight looked cheap, but **hidden costs** like baggage fees doubled the price.
Before you buy a pool, think about the **hidden costs**: chemicals, repairs and a higher water bill.
People often forget the **hidden costs** of a long commute, like lost sleep and less time with family.

drill.sentence: The ad promises a phone plan for twenty dollars a month with no {{hidden costs}}, but I'll believe it when I see the bill.
drill.hint: money you only find out about later (the noun is not *fees* or *charges*)

entries.related: *hidden fees* — very close, common for banks, tickets and hotels; *the fine print* — the small text where such costs are often explained; *all-inclusive* — the opposite, everything is in the price.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To manage to understand something that is confusing, complicated or unclear.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing, often with *try to* or *can't*: *I can't make sense of these instructions.* Don't confuse it with *make sense* without *of*, which means "be logical": *That makes sense.* It is also used for painful events: *make sense of a loss*.
entries.pattern: (try to / can't) make sense of + noun
examples: I've read the tax form three times, and I still can't **make sense of** it.
Children often need time to **make sense of** a death in the family.
Economists are still trying to **make sense of** the sudden drop in home prices.

drill.sentence: My grandmother's handwriting is so messy that nobody in the family can {{make sense of}} her old recipes.
drill.hint: manage to understand — verb + noun + *of* (not *figure out* or *decipher*)

entries.related: *figure out* — informal, understand or solve; *get your head around* — informal, understand something difficult; *be baffled by* — the opposite, completely unable to understand.
